card_surface: Plane's card face follows the Linear-derived minimal idiom but is more conservative than Linear about surfacing VCS state on the compressed card. On board and list layouts a work item card shows: the work item ID prefix, title, priority icon, state pill, assignee avatars, labels, due date, estimate, and cycle/module badges — driven by the Display dropdown 'Display Properties' toggles in the View Options. Linked PR/branch state is NOT a default card-face property in the documented Display Options list (state, priority, assignees, labels, start/due date, estimate, cycle, modules, customers, milestone, releases, custom properties). The most consistent VCS signal that survives compression is the state pill itself — because Plane's GitHub/GitLab Pull Request Automation moves the work item state automatically as the linked PR moves through draft -> open -> approved -> merged, the card's state pill (e.g. 'In Review', 'Done') effectively encodes PR lifecycle without a separate branch glyph. Card-level link count: when sub-work items exist, a small sub-issue count indicator can render; an analogous PR/branch count badge on the card face is not documented as a first-class display property. Branch name, PR title, and CI check details do not render on the card face. [uncertain]
detail_panel: Plane's work item detail surface is either a slide-in 'peek view' panel or the full work item page, both anchored by a right-side properties sidebar organised into collapsible sections: Details (state, priority, assignees, labels, start/due dates, estimate, tracked time), Project structure (cycle, modules, customers, milestone, releases), Custom properties, and Metadata (created by, created on, updated on). Below the description, the activity/links area carries linked GitHub/GitLab Pull Requests and commits as discrete rows added via the integration; each linked PR row carries PR number, title, current PR state (Draft / Open / Review requested / Approved / Merged / Closed), and a link out to the source repository. The header toolbar exposes a 'Copy branch name' action that generates a Git-ready branch string from the user and the work item ID — branch creation is also a frequently-requested addition. Reviewer/review-state surfacing inside the panel is more limited than Linear's: reviewers come through indirectly via the PR row label (Review requested / Approved), not as native avatar pills inside Plane. Test runs are not native; CI check summaries are not rendered as a dedicated tab — CI signals collapse into the PR row's state mapping. Comments, sub-work items, and attachments occupy the body of the panel below the description; the activity feed records integration events (PR opened, merged, closed) inline. [uncertain]
state_coupling: State coupling is the headline feature of Plane's GitHub and GitLab integrations and is configured per-Plane-project (not per-repo or per-branch). After connecting a repository, workspace admins open Pull Request Automation and map the PR lifecycle states to Plane work item states. The available PR states for mapping are: Draft PR created, PR opened, Review requested, PR approved / ready to merge, PR merged, and PR closed without merging. When a PR linked to a work item moves between these lifecycle states, Plane updates the mapped work item state automatically (e.g. 'In Progress' -> 'In Review' -> 'Done'). Sync is bidirectional with GitHub Issues: closing a GitHub issue moves the linked Plane work item to Done, and changes in Plane (requirements or status) show up in GitHub. Linking uses two mechanisms: explicit linking inside Plane, and 'magic keywords' in the PR or commit message that reference the Plane work item ID — when used, Plane posts a confirmation comment back on the PR. Coupling is opt-in (admins must configure the mapping) but designed to be ON for projects that connect a repo; granularity is per-Plane-project, with the same mapping applying across all repos linked to that project. Recent changelog additions (v1.14, v1.15, v1.16) refined the integration and added the ability to link PRs to Epics. State mapping is the entire model — there is no separate 'auto-close on merge' toggle distinct from the merged-state mapping.
draft_vs_ready_state: Draft PRs are a first-class lifecycle state in Plane's GitHub and GitLab automation. The 'Draft PR created' event is listed alongside 'PR opened', 'Review requested', 'Approved', 'Merged', and 'Closed' as a discrete mappable state in Pull Request Automation. This means teams configure exactly what 'draft' means in their workflow (most commonly: keep the work item in 'In Progress' rather than advancing to 'In Review') and then advance the work item only when the PR is moved out of draft to open/ready-for-review. On the card face the distinction is visible only via the work item state pill — Plane does not render a separate draft/ready icon on the compressed card. Inside the detail panel, the linked PR row shows the PR's current lifecycle label (e.g. 'Draft' vs 'Open' vs 'Review requested') sourced from GitHub/GitLab. Because draft and ready are separate triggers in the mapping, draft PRs can be configured to not trigger state changes at all, which matches the Linear behaviour. [uncertain]
review_state: Review state in Plane is surfaced primarily through the PR lifecycle mapping rather than as native reviewer pills inside the Plane UI. The 'Review requested' and 'Approved / ready to merge' lifecycle events are first-class mappable states, so the work item's state pill carries the reviewer signal indirectly — e.g. a state of 'In Review' configured to map to 'Review requested' tells everyone the PR is now awaiting review. The linked PR row in the work item panel shows the PR's current review status as reported by GitHub/GitLab; clicking through opens the PR for full reviewer detail. Plane does NOT render approval counts (e.g. '2/2 approved') or blocking-review badges natively, and reviewer avatars from the SCM do not appear as pills on the card or in the panel sidebar — reviewers are conceptually delegated to the source platform. Plane does have a separate Workflows and Approvals system (an internal approval gate that prevents state transitions until designated approvers accept or reject) but that mechanism is distinct from PR code review — it gates Plane state changes and shows 'Approval pending' on the work item, not GitHub/GitLab PR approvals. [uncertain]
dod_checklist: Plane has no first-class native Definition of Done checklist field. Teams implement DoD through three patterns: (1) inline markdown task lists inside the work item description (the rich text editor supports markdown checkboxes); (2) sub-work items, which Plane treats as first-class work items with their own states, assignees, estimates, and parent breadcrumb — a parent can show a sub-work-item progress count and items can roll up only by state; and (3) work item templates that pre-populate a description (and optionally a set of sub-work items) with a standard DoD checklist when the template is applied. Cross-project parenting is supported: a work item in Project A can be a sub-work item of a work item in Project B. DoD does NOT gate state transitions natively in the description-checklist case; however, Plane's Workflows and Approvals feature can be configured to gate transitions via approver sign-off, which can be used as a DoD-by-approval pattern. Card-face treatment: the sub-work-item count surfaces on the parent card; in-description markdown checklist completion is not surfaced on the card face. There is no completion-percentage ring tied specifically to a DoD checklist. [uncertain]
test_linkage: Plane has no native test management module — no Tests tab, no test execution rows, no coverage badge. Test linkage is delegated to third-party tools and the broader integrations marketplace; community discussions reference test management add-ons but Plane itself ships no first-class test object. CI test results sync indirectly: GitHub/GitLab CI runs against a linked PR are reflected in the PR's lifecycle state (the 'PR approved / ready to merge' transition typically depends on required checks passing on the source platform), so CI pass/fail collapses into the PR row's state in the work item panel and into the mapped work item state. CI pass/fail and test-management linkage are therefore separate axes: PR-side CI is observable via the linked PR row; structured test execution and coverage are not part of the data model. No coverage badge or pass/fail counter renders on the card face or in the panel. [uncertain]
cicd_status: CI/CD status is not surfaced as a first-class card-face element or as a dedicated panel widget in Plane. The CI signal is observable indirectly: GitHub Actions / GitLab CI results gate the PR's lifecycle state on the source platform, and Plane's Pull Request Automation maps 'PR approved / ready to merge' (which on the source platform requires required checks to pass) to a configured Plane work item state. So a green CI pipeline manifests as the work item moving to a 'Ready to Merge' or equivalent mapped state. Individual check names, pipeline names, and progress indicators (building / passed / failed) are not rendered inside Plane. A failing CI run on a linked PR does not auto-flag the work item as at-risk in Plane; users must go to the linked PR to inspect check detail. Plane's own CI/CD (the makeplane/plane repo's GitHub Actions pipeline) is for product builds — distinct from any user-facing CI surfacing inside a Plane project. [uncertain]
release_tagging: Plane offers two release-adjacent containers: Milestones (project-level, time-based delivery checkpoints with status colour indicators — red not started, blue in progress, green completed) and Releases (introduced as a Project Structure property on work items). Work items can be assigned to milestones either from the milestone view ('Link work items') or from the work item via the properties sidebar; the Project structure section of the properties sidebar exposes cycle, modules, customers, milestone, and releases as separate first-class fields. Cycles (Plane's sprint container) and Modules (cross-cutting feature/area groupings) are distinct from releases — cycles can overlap and recur, modules group work by feature/microservice/initiative. Whether release/milestone/cycle badges render on the card face depends on the layout's Display Properties toggles (these are documented as available in the display options list). Plane v1.16 added the ability to link Git pull requests with Epics for release-traceability use cases. A single work item can carry milestone and release independently, and milestones appear as visual markers on timeline/Gantt views. Release Planning is offered as a project template with a structured framework for coordinating multi-team releases. [uncertain]
aggregation: Aggregation in Plane is partial and primarily state-based, not VCS-based. Parent work items with sub-work-items show a sub-issue progress count on the parent based on completed sub-work-item statuses; Epics (Plane's higher-level container) roll up the state of constituent work items and surface progress at the epic level. Modules, Cycles, and Milestones each expose their own progress rollup (percentage complete, burn-down for cycles, status colour for milestones). PR/branch/CI state is NOT rolled up from child stories to a parent feature card — Plane has no documented 'N of M child work items have merged PRs' aggregator. The work-item-state pill on the parent does benefit indirectly from PR automation (since a child's state advances on PR merge, the parent's progress count advances too) but there is no dedicated VCS-rollup badge. This is consistent with the gap identified across the category: Plane, like Linear and Shortcut, leaves VCS rollup as an unsolved problem. [uncertain]
environment_deployment_target: Plane has no first-class environment/deployment-target field on work items. There is no documented 'env: staging' or 'env: production' badge, no deployment timeline widget, and no native CI/CD deployment event ingestion comparable to Linear Releases pipelines or Jira Deployments. The closest constructs are Releases (as a properties-sidebar field linking the work item to a release container) and Milestones (as time-based delivery checkpoints), but neither encodes the actual environment a change has reached. Deployment context, if surfaced at all, would be modelled through custom properties on a work item type (e.g. a 'Reviewer' or 'Environment' custom field added to an issue type) — these are user-defined rather than first-class. Released changelogs (1.14 -> 1.16, including the 2025-10 universal filtering / GitHub Enterprise release) emphasise PR/issue sync rather than deployment-event ingestion. For RTE/PM personas, the available proxy is the work item state itself once it has advanced through a PR-merged mapping. [uncertain]
traceability_completeness: Plane does not surface a composite traceability indicator. There is no single visual element on the card face or in the panel reporting 'this work item has code + tests + DoD + deploy'. Each axis is tracked independently and indirectly: PR/commit links via the GitHub/GitLab integration's linked items; DoD via markdown checklist or sub-work items; tests via third-party integrations; release/milestone via the Project structure properties. The work item state pill — driven by PR Automation — encodes 'code merged' as a proxy when configured. Plane's Workflows and Approvals feature can gate state transitions via designated approver sign-off ('Approval pending' surfaces on the work item) which is the closest mechanism to a gating-on-traceability pattern, but it is approval-based, not VCS-completeness-based. Incomplete traceability does not block state transitions automatically. This positions Plane in the same category as Linear and Shortcut: separate, simple signals over a composite badge, with completeness implied by the work item reaching a Done state with full PR automation enabled. [uncertain]
design_pattern: Plane's design vocabulary explicitly imitates Linear: a clean, modern UI with a minimal card surface and a structured right-side properties sidebar in the detail panel. The card-face pattern compresses to a single state pill + identity glyphs (priority, assignees, labels) — VCS state is not represented by a dedicated branch-fork icon or PR pill on the card face the way Linear surfaces it; instead, PR lifecycle is encoded entirely into the work item's mapped state. In the detail panel, the pattern is: properties sidebar (collapsible sections for Details, Project structure, Custom properties, Metadata) on the right, description + linked items + activity in the body. Linked PRs render as discrete rows with state labels sourced from GitHub/GitLab. The pattern is consistent across work item types (since type is a property, not a separate card template) and across board, list, calendar, and gantt layouts. Empty state for VCS: no PR rows rendered, no placeholder. Plane's choice to lean on state-mapping rather than a separate card glyph is the most conservative pattern in the cohort — it aligns well with Sand's restrained philosophy (single state pill carrying multiple meanings) but offers less at-a-glance differentiation than Linear's branch-fork icon. The Display Properties dropdown gives users per-layout control over what surfaces on the card, treating VCS-adjacent fields as opt-in chrome. [uncertain]
